cooling_items.text:
Heating and cooling within individual suites are provided by in-suite PTAC (Packaged Terminal Air Conditioner) units, which provide electric resistance heating and DX cooling.

PTAC systems offer basic suite-level temperature control; however, they are significantly less efficient than modern heat pump–based systems. Typical PTAC units operate with cooling COP values in the range of approximately 2.5–3.2, while electric-resistance heating sections operate at a COP of approximately 1.0, meaning that one unit of electrical energy produces one unit of heat. By comparison, modern cold-climate air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems can achieve heating and cooling COP values exceeding 4.0 under favorable operating conditions, delivering substantially higher efficiency and lower operating costs.

As PTAC units age, cooling performance may decline due to compressor wear and refrigerant-related servicing requirements, and overall electrical consumption remains high during the heating season due to resistance-based heating.

Given the relatively low heating efficiency and increasing lifecycle costs associated with electric-resistance-based PTAC systems, replacement with a modern air-source heat pump (ASHP) system is recommended in the short term. Transitioning to ASHP technology would significantly improve energy performance, reduce electrical consumption, lower operating costs, and enhance long-term system reliability.

dhw_items.text:
DHW for each suite is served by an individual electric storage-type water heater, typically rated at approximately 3,000 W. These units operate independently and provide hot water directly to each dwelling unit.

Electric resistance water heaters convert electricity directly into heat and operate with a coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0. While this decentralized configuration simplifies distribution and eliminates centralized piping losses, it results in relatively high electrical consumption compared to centralized condensing or heat pump–based systems.

Conversion to a centralized domestic hot water system or the implementation of heat pump water heaters (HPWH) may offer improved energy performance and reduced electrical consumption. However, such an upgrade would require a detailed feasibility assessment, including evaluation of available electrical capacity, spatial constraints, ventilation requirements, and capital cost implications.

Accordingly, further review as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit or dedicated heat pump feasibility study is recommended to determine the technical and economic viability of transitioning to a heat pump–based DHW solution.

measures.measure_title: Convert In-Suite PTAC to Air-Source Heat Pump System
measures.notes: Replace in-suite PTAC units with high-efficiency air-source heat pump systems to improve energy performance, reduce maintenance costs, and support long-term building electrification.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing electric radiator + DX PTAC units with modern air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems. ASHP systems provide both heating and cooling through a high-efficiency refrigeration cycle and eliminate the need for electric resistance heating.

Modern cold-climate ASHP systems can achieve heating and cooling COP values exceeding 4.0–5.0 under favorable conditions, significantly improving energy efficiency compared to electric resistance heating and conventional DX configurations. In addition, improved part-load modulation enhances occupant comfort and reduces peak electrical demand.

The proposed retrofit would improve suite-level temperature control, reduce long-term maintenance costs, and align the building with electrification and decarbonization strategies. Phased implementation may be considered to align with reserve fund planning and suite turnover cycles.

measures.measure_title: Solar PV : Electricity Generation
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

measures.existing_conditions: The building is served by a make-up air (MUA) unit equipped with a gas-fired heating section and fixed or limited-speed supply fan control. The unit provides ventilation air to corridors and common areas but relies primarily on natural gas combustion for winter heating. While the system is functional, gas-fired heating results in ongoing fuel consumption and limits opportunities for electrification and high-efficiency operation.
measures.measure_title: Retrofit Existing MUA to ASHP-Based MUA with VFD (Gas Heating as Backup)
measures.notes: Upgrade the MUA to a heat pump–based system with VFD control while retaining gas heating as backup to reduce gas use and improve energy performance.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends retrofitting the existing MUA unit to operate as an air-source heat pump (ASHP)–based MUA system while retaining the existing gas-fired heating section as a backup for extreme cold-weather conditions. Under the proposed configuration, an ASHP heating and cooling section would be integrated into the existing MUA cabinet (subject to engineering review), allowing the unit to provide high-efficiency heating and cooling through a refrigeration cycle.

New or upgraded variable frequency drives (VFDs) would be installed on the supply fan to enable airflow modulation based on ventilation demand and discharge air temperature requirements. Integration into a Building Automation System (BAS), where available, would allow optimized scheduling, temperature reset, and coordinated system control.

The ASHP system would handle the majority of annual heating and cooling loads, significantly reducing natural gas consumption, while the existing gas-fired section would operate only as supplemental or emergency heat. This hybrid approach improves energy efficiency, supports decarbonization goals, and minimizes capital cost by retaining functional components of the existing unit.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to confirm equipment sizing, electrical service capacity, structural considerations, and integration constraints. The existing gas-fired heating section is recommended to be retained as backup to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO and Enbridge incentives for heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:

measures.existing_conditions: Domestic cold water is currently pressurized by a constant-speed booster pump with a downstream pressure-reducing or regulating valve to maintain setpoint pressure. The valve introduces unnecessary head loss and wastes pumping energy, and the pump operates at full speed even when demand is low.
measures.measure_title: Booster Pump VFD Retrofit
measures.notes: Convert the constant-speed domestic booster pump to VFD control, eliminating throttling losses and matching pressure to demand for significant pump-energy savings.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a variable frequency drive (VFD) on the domestic water booster pump and remove or bypass the pressure regulating valve. The VFD will control pump speed to maintain the desired discharge pressure directly, allowing the pump to slow down during periods of low demand. This reduces energy use, pump wear and noise while maintaining adequate system pressure. Further engineering is required to confirm setpoints, sensor locations and control logic.

measures.existing_conditions: The parking garage air intake is not equipped with a motorized damper. Outdoor air enters the space continuously, which can result in excessive cold air infiltration during winter conditions. This may contribute to lower garage temperatures, increased heating demand where applicable, and reduced occupant comfort near entry points. No active control strategy was observed to regulate intake airflow based on outdoor temperature or operating conditions.
measures.measure_title: Install Motorized Damper for Garage Air Intake
measures.notes: Install a motorized intake damper to reduce winter cold air infiltration and improve garage temperature control while maintaining required ventilation.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a motorized damper at the garage outdoor air intake, integrated with a temperature sensor and control logic to modulate airflow based on outdoor conditions. The damper would reduce unnecessary cold air infiltration during winter while maintaining required ventilation rates. Integration with the existing garage fan controls or BAS (where available) would allow coordinated operation and improved seasonal performance. This measure would help stabilize garage temperatures, reduce potential heating energy demand, and improve occupant comfort near entry areas

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: Common area lighting (e.g., corridors, stairwells, storage rooms, parking areas, and ancillary spaces) is primarily controlled through manual switches or time-based schedules, resulting in lighting operating during unoccupied periods. Limited occupancy-based control leads to unnecessary electrical energy use and increased lamp operating hours.
measures.measure_title: Lighting Motion Sensor Control Retrofit
measures.notes: Install occupancy-based motion sensors for common area lighting to reduce unnecessary runtime, lower electrical consumption, and extend lighting equipment life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends installing occupancy / motion sensors to control common area lighting where appropriate. The motion sensors would automatically turn lighting on when spaces are occupied and off or dim when spaces are unoccupied, reducing unnecessary runtime while maintaining occupant safety and visibility.

This measure would reduce electrical energy consumption, extend lamp and ballast/driver life, and lower ongoing maintenance requirements. Motion control is particularly effective in intermittently occupied spaces such as stairwells, corridors, storage rooms, and parking areas.

Where applicable, motion sensors may be integrated with existing lighting control strategies or future centralized control systems to further enhance operational flexibility.

measures.existing_conditions: Common areas and the garage are illuminated primarily by 4-ft T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spirals controlled by manual switches. These technologies have relatively high energy use and shorter lamp life compared to modern LED lighting.
measures.measure_title: Common Area and Garage Lighting Retrofit
measures.notes: Retrofit T8 and CFL lighting in common areas and garages to LED with occupancy/daylight controls to cut electricity use and maintenance while improving lighting quality.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Mann recommends retrofitting all existing T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spiral lamps with high-efficiency LED fixtures or lamps. LEDs consume significantly less electricity, have a longer lifespan, and reduce maintenance. Occupancy sensors or motion detectors should be installed in garages, mechanical rooms, laundry rooms, and other intermittently used spaces so lights operate only when needed. Daylight sensors can be added where natural light is available. This combined approach can substantially reduce electricity consumption, improve lighting quality and safety, and lower maintenance costs.

The existing make-up air (MUA) unit is equipped with a constant-speed supply fan and an integral gas-fired heating burner, providing heating-only capacity. The unit does not include variable frequency drive (VFD) control and does not provide mechanical cooling.

The absence of VFD control results in fixed airflow operation regardless of actual ventilation demand, limiting part-load efficiency and increasing electrical energy consumption. The gas-fired heating section provides basic winter heating capability; however, without cooling capacity, heat recovery, or advanced modulation control, the system offers limited seasonal optimization and indoor temperature regulation.

At the time of the site visit, the unit was observed to be in functional condition with no visible mechanical deficiencies. However, the configuration reflects an older, conventional ventilation design with limited energy efficiency and control flexibility.

Electric resistance water heaters convert electricity directly into heat and operate with a coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0. While this decentralized configuration simplifies distribution and eliminates centralized piping losses, it results in relatively high electrical consumption compared to centralized condensing or heat pump–based systems.

Conversion to a centralized domestic hot water system or the implementation of heat pump water heaters (HPWH) may offer improved energy performance and reduced electrical consumption. However, such an upgrade would require a detailed feasibility assessment, including evaluation of available electrical capacity, spatial constraints, ventilation requirements, and capital cost implications.

Accordingly, further review as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit or dedicated heat pump feasibility study is recommended to determine the technical and economic viability of transitioning to a heat pump–based DHW solution.
measures.measure_title: Convert In-Suite Electric Water Heaters to Heat Pump Water Heaters (HPWH)
measures.notes: Replace electric water heaters with heat pump water heaters to significantly reduce electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing in-suite electric resistance storage water heaters with high-efficiency heat pump water heaters (HPWH). Heat pump water heaters extract heat from ambient air and transfer it to domestic water, typically achieving COP values in the range of 2.5–4.0, significantly reducing electrical consumption compared to resistance-based systems (COP ≈ 1.0).

This approach maintains the existing decentralized configuration and avoids the substantial capital cost associated with installing a centralized DHW plant, including new boilers, distribution piping, and major mechanical room reconfiguration. Implementation would require review of available electrical capacity, ventilation and air-source requirements, condensate drainage provisions, and space constraints within each suite or mechanical area.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

measures.existing_conditions: The parking garage air intake is not equipped with a motorized damper. Outdoor air enters the space continuously, which can result in excessive cold air infiltration during winter conditions. This may contribute to lower garage temperatures, increased heating demand where applicable, and reduced occupant comfort near entry points. No active control strategy was observed to regulate intake airflow based on outdoor temperature or operating conditions.
measures.measure_title: Install Motorized Damper for Garage Air Intake
measures.notes: Install a motorized intake damper to reduce winter cold air infiltration and improve garage temperature control while maintaining required ventilation.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a motorized damper at the garage outdoor air intake, integrated with a temperature sensor and control logic to modulate airflow based on outdoor conditions. The damper would reduce unnecessary cold air infiltration during winter while maintaining required ventilation rates. Integration with the existing garage fan controls or BAS (where available) would allow coordinated operation and improved seasonal performance. This measure would help stabilize garage temperatures, reduce potential heating energy demand, and improve occupant comfort near entry areas

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: Common area lighting (e.g., corridors, stairwells, storage rooms, parking areas, and ancillary spaces) is primarily controlled through manual switches or time-based schedules, resulting in lighting operating during unoccupied periods. Limited occupancy-based control leads to unnecessary electrical energy use and increased lamp operating hours.
measures.measure_title: Lighting Motion Sensor Control Retrofit
measures.notes: Install occupancy-based motion sensors for common area lighting to reduce unnecessary runtime, lower electrical consumption, and extend lighting equipment life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends installing occupancy / motion sensors to control common area lighting where appropriate. The motion sensors would automatically turn lighting on when spaces are occupied and off or dim when spaces are unoccupied, reducing unnecessary runtime while maintaining occupant safety and visibility.

This measure would reduce electrical energy consumption, extend lamp and ballast/driver life, and lower ongoing maintenance requirements. Motion control is particularly effective in intermittently occupied spaces such as stairwells, corridors, storage rooms, and parking areas.

Where applicable, motion sensors may be integrated with existing lighting control strategies or future centralized control systems to further enhance operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

*Further engineering review is required to finalize sensor locations, control strategy, and integration with existing lighting and electrical systems.

measures.existing_conditions: Common areas and the garage are illuminated primarily by 4-ft T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spirals controlled by manual switches. These technologies have relatively high energy use and shorter lamp life compared to modern LED lighting.
measures.measure_title: Common Area and Garage Lighting Retrofit
measures.notes: Retrofit T8 and CFL lighting in common areas and garages to LED with occupancy/daylight controls to cut electricity use and maintenance while improving lighting quality.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Mann recommends retrofitting all existing T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spiral lamps with high-efficiency LED fixtures or lamps. LEDs consume significantly less electricity, have a longer lifespan, and reduce maintenance. Occupancy sensors or motion detectors should be installed in garages, mechanical rooms, laundry rooms, and other intermittently used spaces so lights operate only when needed. Daylight sensors can be added where natural light is available. This combined approach can substantially reduce electricity consumption, improve lighting quality and safety, and lower maintenance costs.

No widespread outages were observed during the walkthrough, and the overall lighting levels were appropriate for the building’s use. Further savings may be available through continued LED retrofit and the use of occupancy-based controls in selected low-traffic areas. Or installing light control in the parking area.

misc_items.text: In aging buildings, even double-pane window assemblies may experience gradual deterioration of glazing seals over time. Loss of insulating gas or degradation of the sealed air space between panes can reduce overall thermal performance. While the existing windows were observed to be in generally fair condition, it would be prudent to incorporate sealant renewal and eventual glazing upgrades into the building’s long-term capital planning strategy.
misc_items.title: Window condition (Aging double pane)

misc_items.text: The building envelope appears to be in generally fair condition, with no significant signs of air leakage or deterioration observed at the time of the site visit. Envelope components appear to be performing as intended.
misc_items.title: Envelope Condition (Fair)

misc_items.text: The parking garage is served by a mechanical ventilation system controlled by carbon monoxide (CO) sensors. Exhaust fans start and stop in response to measured CO levels, providing demand-based operation and reducing unnecessary runtime during periods of low vehicle activity. The garage fans and control system appeared to be functioning normally, with no obvious mechanical deficiencies reported.
misc_items.title: Garage ventilation (Has CO controls)

misc_items.text: The building includes an unheated parking garage, which is typical for buildings of this age. No dedicated space-heating system was observed, and garage temperatures are allowed to fluctuate with outdoor conditions.
misc_items.title: Unheated garage

ventilation_items.text:
The existing make-up air (MUA) unit is equipped with a constant-speed supply fan and an integral gas-fired heating burner, providing heating-only capacity. The unit does not include variable frequency drive (VFD) control and does not provide mechanical cooling.

The absence of VFD control results in fixed airflow operation regardless of actual ventilation demand, limiting part-load efficiency and increasing electrical energy consumption. The gas-fired heating section provides basic winter heating capability; however, without cooling capacity, heat recovery, or advanced modulation control, the system offers limited seasonal optimization and indoor temperature regulation.

At the time of the site visit, the unit was observed to be in functional condition with no visible mechanical deficiencies. However, the configuration reflects an older, conventional ventilation design with limited energy efficiency and control flexibility.
